Promoting Environmental Sustainability Through Tree Plantation and Community Participation

A six-week Community Service Project in Gudur village, Andhra Pradesh: surveying households, talking about trees, and planting saplings with local residents.

  • Gudur, Andhra PradeshProject community
  • 1 June – 26 July 2026Project period
  • Sree Venkateswara College of EngineeringNellore (Autonomous)

Potting a sapling at a household in Gudur.

Project overview

Trees clean the air, hold soil in place, give shade and shelter wildlife. Growing construction, tree cutting and low awareness have reduced green space in many villages, Gudur included.

Our project set out to change that locally. We observed the village, found places where trees could grow, surveyed residents, ran awareness conversations, and planted saplings together with the community, then went back to see how they were doing.

The main message: protecting the environment is not only a job for government. It is shared by every household, and planting is only the start. Saplings need watering, protection and someone who takes responsibility for them.

  • Environmental awareness
  • Teamwork
  • Leadership
  • Communication
  • Survey skills
  • Social responsibility

What we set out to do

  • Raise awarenessExplain how trees reduce air pollution, give oxygen, prevent soil erosion and support biodiversity.
  • Listen to residentsUse a 12-question survey and household visits to learn what people know and what stops them planting.
  • Plant with the communityChoose suitable places and saplings, and plant alongside local people rather than for them.
  • Make care a habitShow why watering, fencing and regular care decide whether a sapling survives.

About Gudur

Gudur is a residential village where farmers, small business owners, private and government employees, daily-wage workers and students live side by side. It has homes, roads, schools, shops and the basic facilities people need every day.

Residents keep their customs, festivals and family ties, and share values that suit a plantation drive well.

  • Respect for elders and family
  • Helping neighbours
  • Joining local festivals and gatherings
  • Keeping public places clean
  • Respecting nature
  • Unity and cooperation

Six weeks, step by step

Each week had one clear aim, from choosing the site to checking on the saplings.

  1. Week 1 · 1–6 June

    Getting to know the village

    Visited Gudur, observed trees and open spaces, marked possible plantation spots (roadsides, school surroundings, gardens) and drafted the survey questionnaire.

  2. Week 2 · 8–13 June

    Household survey

    Went door to door to ask about trees near homes, awareness of their benefits, interest in planting, and problems like tree cutting and poor upkeep.

  3. Week 3 · 15–20 June

    Awareness conversations

    Explained how trees clean the air and give oxygen, why existing trees should not be cut, and why saplings need regular watering.

  4. Week 4 · 22–27 June

    Planning the plantation

    Revisited the shortlisted places, spoke to residents about the difficulties of planting, and studied native species suited to local soil and climate.

  5. Week 5 · 29 June – 4 July

    Planting with residents

    Arranged saplings, prepared the sites and planted together with community members, then agreed who would look after each tree.

  6. Week 6 · 6–11 July

    Follow-up and feedback

    Checked the saplings, collected feedback, and noted challenges such as water availability and protection from damage.

What we found

Problems in the community

  • Too few trees and green spaces in some parts of the village
  • Trees cut for construction and other activities
  • Low awareness about tree plantation
  • Rising dust and vehicle pollution, and higher heat as green cover shrinks
  • Saplings left without protection or regular watering
  • Limited resident, school and youth participation
  • Plastic waste dumped in open areas

What the project achieved

  • Residents understand more clearly why trees matter
  • People are more willing to plant and protect saplings
  • Students and young people showed interest in environmental work
  • Places needing extra greenery were identified
  • Residents recognised their own role in keeping trees alive
See the 12 survey questions
  1. Are you aware of the importance of tree plantation?
  2. Do you have trees or plants around your house?
  3. Do you think trees help reduce air pollution?
  4. Have you participated in any tree plantation programme?
  5. Are you interested in planting saplings in your surroundings?
  6. Do you know the importance of protecting existing trees?
  7. Is there enough greenery in your village?
  8. What are the main reasons for cutting down trees in your area?
  9. Are people in your village interested in environmental protection activities?
  10. Who should take responsibility for maintaining planted saplings?
  11. Would you participate in future tree plantation programmes?
  12. What suggestions would you give to make your village greener?

What should happen next

Recommendations for residents, the school and the Gram Panchayat.

Short term

  • Hold awareness programmes on trees and the environment
  • Plant in schools, along roadsides and in public places
  • Give saplings to interested families
  • Water and protect new saplings regularly
  • Put up posters and banners

Long term

  • Every household plants and looks after at least one tree
  • Yearly plantation programmes
  • Local groups that monitor tree growth and survival
  • Ask the Gram Panchayat for saplings and watering support
  • Stop unnecessary tree cutting
  • Regular environmental sessions in schools

Conclusion

Tree plantation is not only about planting trees but also about protecting and maintaining them. When students, youth and residents work together, a village can grow greener, healthier and more sustainable for the next generation.
